title: Avalanches
summary: Slab avalanches are the leading natural cause of death for backcountry travellers. Most are triggered by the victim or their party.
signs: Recent heavy snowfall or rapid warming
tips: Read the avalanche bulletin every day, and match the terrain to the danger rating.
Carry a transceiver, probe and shovel, and practise rescue until it is fast and calm.
Cross suspect slopes one at a time; regroup only in safe zones.
Avalanche airbags help, but they are never a substitute for good decisions.

title: Altitude Sickness
summary: Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS) can progress to life-threatening High Altitude Pulmonary Edema (HAPE) or Cerebral Edema (HACE). Anyone can be affected above 2,500 m.
signs: HAPE: breathlessness at rest, wet cough
tips: Ascend gradually and sleep low; build in rest days.
Descend at the first signs of HAPE or HACE: descent is the definitive treatment.
Carry and know how to use dexamethasone, nifedipine and oxygen where guidelines allow.
Never ascend with symptoms of AMS.

title: Crevasses
summary: Glaciers flow, and as they flex they crack. Snow bridges can hide crevasses tens of metres deep and give no warning until they collapse.
signs: Sagging or depressed lines in the snow
tips: Always rope up on glaciers; keep the rope taut and spaced properly.
Travel early, when snow bridges are still frozen.
Practise crevasse rescue (pulley systems, Z-pulley, drop-loop) before you need it.
Probe doubtful areas and cross bridges at right angles.

title: Weather
summary: Mountain weather changes rapidly. Wind, whiteouts, lightning and sudden storms are involved in a large proportion of serious mountaineering incidents.
signs: Rapid pressure drops on an altimeter watch
tips: Study multiple forecasts; add a mountain-specific forecast for the exact summit elevation.
Start early, so you are descending before afternoon convection builds.
Set a firm turnaround time, and be willing to retreat.
In an electrical storm, move off exposed ridges and keep away from metal gear.

title: Rockfall
summary: Warming temperatures free rocks locked in ice, and climbers above can dislodge stones. A helmet is the most basic and effective protection you can wear.
signs: Fresh debris at the base of gullies
Mid-day thaw after a cold night
tips: Always wear a helmet, even on approaches.
Avoid gullies and the fall line of parties above you.
Shout 'Rock!' immediately and flatten to the face if something comes down.
Climb early while the ice still glues the mountain together.

title: Sérac Collapse
summary: Blocks of glacier ice up to the size of houses calve without warning. They are the biggest objective hazard on glaciated routes and have killed entire teams instantly.
signs: Blue ice and recent collapse debris below
tips: Cross glacier zones quickly and never linger below an icefall or a hanging glacier.
Camp well away from sérac faces and beneath obvious avalanche paths.
Follow the route of the last collapse debris and treat any ground above it as suspect.
Spread out in exposed zones so one collapse does not take the whole team.

title: Snow Blindness
summary: Snow blindness is sunburn of the cornea. It is entirely preventable, painfully easy to get, and the cause of many otherwise avoidable descents.
signs: Burning or gritty eyes after a bright ascent
tips: Wear category 4 glacier glasses whenever there is snow on the ground, cloud or not.
Wear them while the eyes are closed or asleep: snow blindness often happens overnight.
Carry a spare pair. A broken or lost pair of glacier glasses is a genuine emergency.
If the eyes are affected, rest in shade, do not rub, and expect full recovery in 24–48 hours.

title: Hypothermia & Frostbite
summary: Cold is a slow and silent adversary. Wind chill, wet clothing and exhaustion can drop core temperature, and exposed skin freezes quickly at altitude.
tips: Layer for moisture management: wicking base, insulating mid, windproof shell.
Keep hands, feet and face covered; spare mitts weigh almost nothing.
Eat and drink regularly; the body burns fuel to stay warm.
Warm gently, never rub frostbitten skin, and avoid refreezing.
